item.title: Evaluation of Image Noise from Computed Tomography in an Organ-Specific Anthropomorphic Phantom
item.description: arXiv:2611.07357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is used ubiquitously for diagnostic imaging, with novel iterative reconstructions such as hybrid iterative reconstruction with partial model-based component (ASiR-V) and deep learning image reconstruction (DLIR) increasingly utilized. In conjunction, CT vendors have developed a noise index (NI) to reduce radiation dose during protocol development. However, it is unclear how these reconstruction algorithms reduce noise as NI changes, particularly across multiple organs. The goal of this study was to utilize an anthropomorphic phantom to evaluate image noise against the prescribed NI across different organs, determine if DLIR reduces image noise compared to ASiR-V, and use this relationship to determine the maximum volume CT dose index (CTDIvol) reduction at equivalent noise levels. Repeat images were acquired on a GE HealthCare Revolution Apex CT scanner across NI values in an anthropomorphic adult-sized phantom from Kyoto Kagaku with ASiR-V and DLIR. Organs-of-interest were contoured using TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer. The correlation between the CTDIvol and NI was determined. The standard deviation of the difference in the repeat images was used as a noise metric (NM), correlated with NI, used to determine the NI at equivalent NM between ASiR-V and DLIR, then applied to determine the dose reduction and difference in NM. The relationship between NI and the resulting CTDIvol was found to be proportional to a power law of exponent -2.23. The maximum potential absolute dose reduction from using DLIR was found in the liver at 1.3 mGy with an NI of 7.9. Across all organs, the relative dose reduction increased, the NM-to-NI ratio decreased, and the noise reduction increased across NI. The relationship between image noise and the prescribed NI differed between ASiR-V and DLIR and varied by organ, with model-based dose reductions of up to 1.3 mGy in the liver.
item.dc:creator: Lucas McCullum, Mojtaba Zarei, Andy Tsai, Michael J. Callahan, Peng Sun, Da Zhang

item.title: High resolution 3D localization of ultrasound sparse sources using a SAGE algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.07966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable localization and characterization of cavitation activity are central to many ultrasound imaging and therapy monitoring applications. Passive acoustic mapping (PAM) can estimate cavitation distributions without prior assumptions but remains limited by the system point spread function. While advanced PAM methods improve spatial resolution, their performance may degrade for transient emissions with uncertain emission times. In this work, we propose a parametric source localization framework based on the Space-Alternating Generalized Expectation-Maximization (SAGE) algorithm to estimate source positions and emitted waveforms directly from array channel data. A greedy source extraction and localization procedure is first used to initialize the model order and source parameters, after which SAGE iteratively refines each source estimate. The proposed method was validated on 49 simulated acquisitions containing up to seven simultaneously emitting sources with emission time uncertainties of 12 microseconds, achieving a source localization precision of 0.24 mm (standard deviation of the total localization error). Experimental evaluation on proton-induced nanodroplet vaporization data acquired with an ultrasound matrix array demonstrated improved spatial resolution compared to a beamforming-based approach and sub-millimeter agreement between vaporization maps and the proton distribution in all three spatial dimensions. These results highlight the potential of parametric source localization for high-resolution proton therapy monitoring and provide a general framework for the localization of simultaneously emitting sparse ultrasound sources.
item.dc:creator: Sophie V. Heymans, Fran\c{c}ois Rottenberg, Tatiana Gelvez-Barrera, Adrian Basarab, Barbara Nicolas

item.title: Continuous Space-Time Finite Element Simulations for Biomedical Flows with Large Boundary Motion and Time-Periodicity
item.description: arXiv:2611.07822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an axisymmetric continuous simplex space-time finite element method for incompressible fluid flow. Compared to conventional time-stepping methods, the space-time approach has several advantages. First, the motion of the domain is incorporated into the space-time geometry, allowing for large boundary motion without remeshing or projection of the solution. Second, the method allows for time-periodic solutions to be computed directly, without the need to simulate multiple cycles. Third, the space-time mesh can be partitioned in time as well as in space, which enables parallelism in time. The method is demonstrated on an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) in a rigid tube. The balloon inflation is modelled based on measured data, and includes a travelling wave along the balloon. The method is able to resolve complex flow features such as jets and recirculation zones. A refinement study shows convergence under temporal, spatial and combined space-time refinement. In weak scaling tests up to 960 ranks, the cost per solver iteration remains approximately constant, and partitioning the mesh into time slabs improves the convergence of the linear solver compared to partitions that cut through both space and time.
item.dc:creator: Nico Dirkes, Marek Behr

item.title: Resampling-based batch reweighting for ComBat harmonization of MRI radiomic features in a multi-scanner glioma cohort
item.description: arXiv:2611.02156v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Radiomic features derived from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are sensitive to scanners; therefore, they require harmonization across scanners. In a radiomic feature dataset, some batches may be severely underrepresented compared to the others e.g., the Erasmus Glioma Database, which may provide harmonized features biased towards the larger batches in the dataset. We investigated whether reweighting underrepresented scanner batches before empirical-Bayes ComBat estimation improves feature harmonization and reduces residual scanner association while retaining grade-related information. In this retrospective, the Erasmus Glioma Database included 733 eligible patients acquired at a single center across nine vendor-by-field-strength configurations. Structural MRI acquired at 1 T, 1.5 T, and 3 T; four structural MRI sequences were analyzed. From four structural MRI sequences, 428 features were computed using an IBSI-compliant PyRadiomics implementation. The sample sizes of some scanner batches were very small compared to others, which may produce unequal precision and shrinkage of batch-effect estimates. We proposed a data augmentation approach to overcome the limitation of ComBat. We provided exploratory evidence, along with confirmatory Kruskal-Wallis tests with a Benjamini-Hochberg correction to assess the proposed method. Before harmonization, 392/428 features (91.6%) differed significantly across scanner batches (median eta-squared=0.463). Standard ComBat reduced this to 13/428 (3.0%), whereas batch-augmented ComBat reduced it to 8/428 (1.9%); the median residual effect size was <0.001 for both harmonized conditions. Batch augmentation appeared to be a useful strategy to improve the performance of ComBat for feature harmonization under severe batch-size imbalance.
item.dc:creator: Rifa Sajda Tasnim, Yushuf Sharker, Md Forhad Hossain, Rakibur Rahman, Enamul Hoque Bhuiyan
